newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - This time, the Samaritans need the help.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - This time, the Samaritans need the help.

text.p: "Whatever you're going through, we'll go through it with you." That's the slogan of the Samaritans, the British charity that lends a sympathetic ear to people going through crisis or at risk of suicide.
But the listening charity has its own problems, finding it harder to match dwindling volunteers with an ever-increasing demand for the service.

"It's a bit chicken and egg," vice-chairwoman Jean Mann told Reuters. "We are so very busy now and volunteers would really like to stay but are finding it hard to cope with the high number of calls and a demanding job."

The Samaritans have lost eight percent of their volunteers over the last two years, but calls have soared by 23 percent this decade. Volunteers answer more than 3.75 million calls each year from distressed people.
As a result, the charity has launched a its biggest ever advertising campaign, costing 100,000 pounds ($160,000), in a bid to attract 10,000 new recruits.
Mann, who became a Samaritan in 1982, believes people were beginning to realise that a problem shared could sometimes be a problem halved.
"Talking about your feelings isn't a weakness. It means that you're taking care of yourself," she said.
She should know.

Some 15 years ago, she was living under the cloud of a life-threatening illness. Prompted by this to use her remaining life to some purpose, she walked into her local Samaritans office and offered her help.
"I had a lovely marriage, lovely children, but I had always hoped that there would be space to do something else for me," she said.
"I came to the Samaritans and said: 'Look, I dont know how much longer I've got, but can I help you?' I did and I'm still here."
Mann made a full recovery and is now the Samaritans' vice-chairwoman.
She has no regrets. She talks animatedly about her work, using words like "wonderful" and "invigorating" and believes the potential gains far outweigh the effort Samaritans put in.
"Most people want to help others because they have a need to be helpful and useful," she says. "In return, we give our volunteers a lot of joy and confidence in their lives."
WHAT SAMARITANS DO

The Samaritans ask for no particular qualifications, although the selection process is quite rigid. Potential volunteers who call a special number are invited to an open evening at their nearest branch.
They can sign up for a longer interview and then if the idea still appeals, they would start a prep course.
"You learn a lot about yourself and your prejudices. If you survive that then you can start probationary duties at your local branch," said Mann.
So what does a Samaritan do?
"You have to be able to talk to the abused and the abuser with equal compassion; talking to the battered wife and the husband who's doing the battering without being judgmental is tough," she said.
The Samaritans dont offer advice. Mann says that doesn't work. Neither does blackmail.
"If someone has just taken an overdose, you can't tell them to think of their children. You just talk to them and hope they begin to trust you".

Presented with a caller who has attempted suicide, most people would want to get help immediately, and Mann agrees that the Samaritans would endeavour to act quickly. But what if the caller refuses to co-operate?
"We'd try to persuade; try to find a reason why they should accept help, but it would be wrong to persuade them to do something they didn't want to do.
"We'd try to convince them that they do have a friend in you; that they have someone to talk to and share problems with and yes, you do care."
But Mann admits that there are tragic occasions when volunteers realise that a caller does not want to choose life.
"There are people who just want someone to talk to while they die."
Rather than forcing through their own solutions, Samaritans encourage callers to open up and suggest their own ways of coping with their problems.
"You're giving them a chance to talk about improving their situation if that's what they want. If they dont, then you just listen and accept what they tell you."
Nowadays her main tasks include fund-raising, publicity, and "reaching out" to high-risk areas.
Farmers have been vulnerable since the "mad cow" scare in Britain plunged thousands into poverty.
The medical profession is another high risk group.
"They see themselves as providing a service to the community, and when it all goes wrong, they have the means to take their own life," said Mann.
But is it all too much to bear?
"I've shed many tears, yes. Sometimes it's very, very sad. I've never felt fed up but I've felt tired at times and wondered if I could go on."
Mann says Samaritans help each other through tough times. Although the service is confidential, volunteers offload problems within the four walls of a branch.

"And there's sometimes such joy. Just by talking to someone you can give them the strength to go on, go back and have another try, live long enough to come through a situation. I comfort myself always with the fact that if no-one was here they wouldn't have had anyone to talk to.
"I'm convinced lives have been saved or made more bearable through the Samaritans. I wouldn't have given it 15 years if I thought it wasn't working."
